memo.executiveSummary: Ledger & Lyric Bookkeeping is a remote QuickBooks Online practice for working musicians, podcasters, and YouTube creators, most of them in Nashville, with 31 clients on monthly retainers plus cleanup projects. 2025 revenue was $52,000, up 4 percent, with owner earnings of about $27,000. The owner is taking an in-house finance role and is asking $48,000.
memo.businessOverview: Clients send receipts through Dext and connect bank feeds to QuickBooks Online; the owner categorizes, reconciles, and delivers a monthly report with a 20-minute call. Royalty statements from ASCAP, BMI, and DistroKid are mapped into a custom chart of accounts the owner built, which transfers with the practice. An overflow contractor handles about 20 percent of monthly closes. Billing runs through Stripe for 16 clients and ACH or Zelle for the rest; two Nashville CPAs refer clients and receive tax-prep handoffs in return.
memo.industryAndMarket: Nashville's music economy produces thousands of 1099 earners with irregular royalty and touring income who are underserved by generalist bookkeepers. Creator-economy income keeps growing nationally, and remote delivery means the client base is not limited to Tennessee.
growthOpportunities: Move all clients to Stripe billing and raise the base retainer to $150, which three clients already pay
Package quarterly estimated-tax planning as a $75 add-on
Pursue a referral agreement with a Nashville music-management firm the owner has already spoken with
memo.transitionPlan: The owner will co-deliver two full monthly close cycles with the buyer and introduce every client by video call, then stay available for questions through the January 1099 season. QuickBooks Accountant, Dext, Stripe, and the domain transfer at closing, and both referring CPAs have agreed to meet the buyer.

memo.executiveSummary: Cherry Street Second Edition is an 11-year-old used bookstore on Tulsa's Cherry Street with about 22,000 titles, a trade-in credit program, a small coffee bar, and online sales of collectible and out-of-print titles. 2025 revenue was $118,000, down 9 percent, with owner earnings of about $22,400. The owner is turning 70 and is asking $41,000 for the inventory, fixtures, lease, and name.
memo.businessOverview: The store occupies 1,400 sq ft at $2,000 a month on a lease through June 2027, open six days a week with two part-time booksellers covering 40 hours between them. Trade-ins are credited at 25 percent of resale value through Square's customer directory; higher-value titles are listed on AbeBooks and eBay from a back-room desk. A four-seat coffee bar serves drip and pastries from a nearby bakery. Monthly author readings and a book club bring in 30 to 50 people and are promoted on Instagram and a 2,400-address Mailchimp list.
memo.industryAndMarket: Tulsa's Cherry Street district draws steady weekend foot traffic from restaurants and the farmers market, and independent bookstores nationally have grown in count since 2019. Used-book margins depend on trade-in flow and curation; the main local competition is a large Gardner's outlet and the online marketplaces.
growthOpportunities: Restore the Sunday and evening hours cut in 2025, which coincide with the revenue decline
Grow online sales, since the AbeBooks desk lists fewer than 600 of the store's collectible titles
Expand the coffee bar and events, which carry the highest margin per square foot
memo.transitionPlan: The owner will work in the store for six weeks to teach buying, pricing, and the AbeBooks workflow, and will introduce the landlord and the bakery supplier. The lease assignment requires landlord consent, which the owner has requested in writing; both booksellers plan to stay.

memo.executiveSummary: Front Range Deed Watch is a weekly paid newsletter that summarizes notable property transfers, permit filings, and zoning actions across Denver, Jefferson, and Arapahoe counties for agents, investors, and curious neighbors. 2025 revenue was $20,000, up 26 percent, with owner earnings of $8,000 after paying a contract researcher. The owner is moving to Portugal and is asking $16,000.
memo.businessOverview: Each Thursday issue is built from county assessor and recorder exports, Denver's permit portal, and planning-board agendas, assembled by a part-time researcher in a shared Google Sheet and written up by the owner in about three hours. The newsletter runs on Ghost Pro with Stripe billing, 540 paying subscribers, and a free list of 4,900 that receives a monthly teaser issue. Sponsorships are sold to two title companies and a mortgage broker at $350 per issue slot. The owner spends about eight hours a week in total.
memo.industryAndMarket: Denver's housing market generates constant interest in who is buying what, and no local outlet covers property records at the neighborhood level. Paid local newsletters have proven durable in metros of this size, and the subscriber base skews toward agents and investors who expense the cost.
growthOpportunities: Add Boulder and Douglas counties, which readers request most often
Sell a quarterly data export to brokerages at a higher price point
Raise the annual price to $50; the current $40 has not changed since launch
memo.transitionPlan: The owner will co-write four issues with the buyer and document the county data sources, the researcher's workflow, and the sponsorship contacts. Ghost, Stripe, the domain, and the researcher's contract transfer at closing.
